definition: The distant past, especially the age of the ancient Greeks and Romans.
example: Some of the city's roads still follow routes that were first laid out in antiquity.
nuance: Antiquity names an era long gone, while an antique is a single old object that may be only a century old.
prompt: A museum guide introduces a hall of carved marble statues.
options: The guide explained that the statues were carved in antiquity for a seaside temple.
The guide hoped the statues would be preserved so that antiquity could admire them.
The guide said the marble was quarried in antiquity, sometime around the late 1990s.
The guide pointed out the antiquity of the gift shop's brand-new postcards.
reasons: Statues made for an ancient temple belong to the far-off era this word describes.
Future generations are posterity; this word looks backward in time, not forward.
A few decades ago is recent history, far too modern to count as the ancient world.
Freshly printed postcards have no great age, so calling attention to their age makes no sense.

practice.prompt: A student is writing a report on the history of mathematics.
options: Scholars in antiquity estimated the size of the Earth with surprising accuracy.
Her report predicted that pocket calculators would become common in antiquity.
She described last spring's school math fair as a famous event of antiquity.
Her teacher praised the antiquity of the report, calling it clear and well organized.
reasons: Thinkers working thousands of years ago lived in the ancient era the word refers to.
A prediction points to the future, but the word names an age that ended long ago.
Something that happened a year ago is far too recent to belong to the ancient past.
Clarity and good organization are qualities of writing, not signs of great age.
